John Baird defends Canadian health care after Trump raises 'boogeyman'

Former foreign affairs minister John Baird is defending the Canadian health-care system following Donald Trump's assertion in the U.S. presidential debate that it's catastrophically bad.

The former Conservative cabinet minister also warned the world is heading into uncharted waters with the rise of American protectionism, which has spiked along with the rise in popularity of Trump, the Republican presidential nominee, and Vermont senator Bernie Sanders, who ran against Hillary Clinton for the Democratic nomination.

Trump dumps on Canada's health care system

Trump’s claim about medical tourism suggestion is not new, and is often evoked by critics of universal health care in Canada and elsewhere. But there’s limited data available on that — and when you look at the best data available, it turns out Trump’s argument was offside.

The most authoritative source studying Canadian-U.S. medical tourism, as Vox pointed out, was a 2002 peer-reviewed, CIHR-funded paper in the journal Health Affairs called ‘Phantoms in the Snow‘. Out of 18,000 Canadian respondents from the National Population Health Survey, only 90 said they had received medical care in the U.S.; just 20 said they had travelled to the States specifically for health services.

“Surprisingly few Canadians travel to the United States for health care, despite the persistence of the myth,” the journal authors write. “For more than a decade, anecdotal reports of waiting lists for elective procedures in Canada and of hordes of Canadian ‘Medicare refugees’ crossing the border in search of medical care in the United States have provided emotive fuel for critics of the Canadian health care system from both sides of the border.”

The comments were especially interesting given that, last year, Trump said in a Fox News debate with other GOP presidential contenders that single-payer healthcare “works in Canada” and “incredibly well in Scotland.” Sen. Rand Paul even attacked him over those comments — although Trump subsequently said he wants a private system “without the artificial lines around every state.”
